header.title: Poematum De Mosaicae Historiae Gestis Libri Quinque: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Avitus Viennensis Episcopus
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp963.tmp963.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

Typesetting slips read through: frudem = fraudem, ct = et, tenUem = tentent, Mir i = Marsi (the Marsian snake-charmers), presenscrit = praesenserit, veuenis = venenis, ei = et. noia is read as nova, 'new things' (it could also be nota, 'known things'). The poem is printed as one paragraph and translated as one.

Typesetting slips read through: projeclam = projectam, doctoa = doctos, funcreo = funereo; nolo is read as noto, 'familiar'. The opening of one verse (',. it, movens') is corrupt, shown as [...]. luminum, 'of lights', makes no sense and is taken as a corruption for a word meaning tricks or illusions. The syntax of 'Tum mandat ... minister' is obscure; longinqua hastilia is taken as 'long staffs' and Aegypti with 'art'.

nodes.text: Now who could worthily describe the fraud of magic, which with silent heart tries out hidden powers and longs to be joined to divine powers? As once the law-giving prophet, under the proud king, while he was showing the new wonders of the sign he had been commanded to give, stirred the magicians with envy, so that they attempted such things and heaped up their own ruin with burning zeal. If right power had perhaps been at their disposal, they would hasten to take away the prodigies, not also to add to them. But their wrath, rivalling the signs only and not equal in power, doubled — the more justly — what it could not remove. Hence it is that the Marsi prevail by their vaunted chant, when with silent art they draw out savage serpents, though absent, and often bid them fight with them. Then, as each perceives a water-snake grievous in battle, or recognises the closed ears of the hard asp, he shakes within him the weapons of a secret spell; and at once, the venoms worn out by the struggling word, soon the disarmed snake is handled with impunity, and in the serpent only the bite, not the poison, is feared. Sometimes the enchanter perishes, if the deaf serpent has scorned the cunning murmurs of the adjurer. It is from the mother, and from the first origin, that they draw this: that, so skilled in the serpent's fraud and tongue, they return in semblance a mutual exchange of speech. No less does a care contrary to salvation assail those whom the foreknown end of their allotted span torments, when they think that shades brought up from the infernal seats join in conversation and report new things. But the spirit of error, which raves in them, prepares answers to their questions with empty figures. And, not to tell each thing in drawn-out speech: deluded in the present, he will be condemned by everlasting judgment, whoever tries to learn what is forbidden.

The law-giving hero happened to be carrying a rod in his hand; leaning on this staff while his right hand guided his step, he flung it down, cast out before him with a strong throw. Then — wonderful to tell — the wood stirred and began to creep: not as it puts forth from the shoot branches without sense, [...] moving only the fruits it makes grow, but creeping in a coil, and, by the use of a changed body, bearing sense and soul, the rod began to run along, and soon, reshaped, it presents a snake. Terrified, he stood fixed, and the tyrant, black for eternity, then turned pale in the face. But lest his attendant, standing by with wavering look, should see him confounded and yielding to such a sign, he conceals that he believes the thing was done by the highest command, wishing the deeds to be thought not divine but [mere illusions]. Then he orders whatever magicians, or men learned in spells, attempt with dire frauds the unlawful art of Egypt, to bring forth long staffs, compelling that his minister perform with funereal murmur the things that had been shown. Then, as ordered, they run together from all sides, and each arms his enchanted staff with the familiar charm; thrown down, they give empty appearances, and the supposed snakes frighten deluded eyes with a deceiving shape. Nor did the magicians swell [with pride] for long: all that they thought they had made is consumed; for the first horned snake, still biting, swallowed in its mouth the serpents feigned by art. After Moses closed the display of power, and, holding the victor by the tail, lifted it from the ground, the serpent gives way to wood, its face withdraws, and the wandering coils stiffened as the body hardened. Why say more? It becomes the former rod, with which the priest afterwards showed very many signs in the time that followed.
